worst_places.before: `setTimeout(fn, 16)` schedules `fn` to run *approximately* every 16ms, but it has no idea when the browser is actually about to paint — it can fire mid-frame, get throttled in background tabs to 1x per second (some browsers), or drift because timers are minimum-delay, not exact-delay. `requestAnimationFrame(fn)` instead asks the browser to call `fn` right before the next repaint, synced to the display's actual refresh rate (typically 60Hz, but 120Hz on newer displays) — so the timing always matches what will actually be shown.

SharedArrayBuffer needs two response headers: `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`. The reason is Spectre.

A Spectre attack measures tiny timing differences to work out what is stored in memory it is not allowed to read directly — a timing side-channel. Shared memory plus a precise clock is exactly the pair of tools such an attack needs. So browsers only hand SharedArrayBuffer out when the page is isolated.

patterns: Background-first leads. About a third of the 35 answers (q-4, q-6, q-10, q-14, q-16, q-17, q-20, q-23, q-26, q-27, q-28, q-34) open with a paragraph on how the browser behaves *by default*, or on the older/worse alternative, and only name the thing the question asked about in sentence two or in paragraph two. Because browser-runtime has no theory article, a reader who reads only the first screen on a phone leaves with the setup and not the answer. The fix is mechanical: move the existing 'X is …' sentence to the front and keep the default-behaviour paragraph underneath as the 'why'.

Difficulty inversely tracks example placement. Junior and middle answers put code within 2-3 sentences of the lead and are genuinely easy to follow; every `advanced` answer (q-28…q-35) front-loads two or three ~200-word paragraphs introducing 5-8 new terms and only then shows code. So the entries with the most new vocabulary are exactly the ones with the least support — and there is no article behind them. q-21 and q-22 are the same failure at senior level (5 and 7 consecutive paragraphs with no code, diagram or table).

Facts are appended to a sentence with a dash instead of being split into sentences. The recurring shape is `main claim — extra fact 1, extra fact 2, or extra fact 3`, and it is what produces every one of the top-8 longest sentences in both locales (60-104 words). No technical detail needs to be cut to fix this: one dash-clause becomes one sentence.

The English version is consistently harder than the Russian, not just longer: 52.8% of en sentences exceed 25 words versus 36.2% of ru over 28, and en leans on idioms and phrasal verbs above B1-B2 — "fair game", "piggyback through", "hand-rolling a protocol", "pegging a core", "sits in waiting", "bails out", "sidestep the whole problem", "blowing the frame budget", "design smell", "neutered" (in a code comment in q-10).

Terminology is not shared between the two files, so the same concept looks like two concepts: кеш/кэш, листенер/слушатель/прослушиватель/обработчик, origin/источник, and Critical Rendering Path rendered three different ways across the ru quiz alone ("Critical Rendering Path" in quiz-8, «критический путь отрисовки» in quiz-11, «критический путь рендеринга» in quiz-18). Section headings in the ru question bank are also left untranslated (### Event Delegation, ### Web Workers, ### CSS Containment, ### Hidden Classes и Inline Caching), as are the inline «Use case:» and «Workflow диагностики» labels.
notes:
Outside the readability rubric but the most important thing found: browser-runtime-quiz-10 marks localStorage as the correct place for auth tokens and its explanation calls HttpOnly cookies "less flexible for logout scenarios" — directly contradicting quiz-13, and contradicting q-3 and q-12, whose whole point is that a token in localStorage is the classic XSS mistake. One of those two quiz items is teaching the anti-pattern as the right answer.
The quiz bank is also heavily duplicated: 19 items cover about 6 topics (reflow/repaint in quiz-1, 6, 12; event delegation in quiz-2, 7, 14, 17; Critical Rendering Path in quiz-8, 11, 18; CORS in quiz-3, 9, 20; token storage in quiz-10, 13; service-worker offline in quiz-15, 19). `browser-runtime-quiz-16` is missing from the id sequence.
Many quiz explanations end with a blanket "The other options misunderstand …" / «Остальные варианты неправильно понимают …» without saying which claim is false — for the reader who picked a distractor, that sentence carries no information.
The question bank contains no diagrams at all (one ASCII process tree in q-25); q-21 and q-22 are precisely where a pipeline diagram would carry the load an article normally carries.
No answer says "as covered in the theory", so nothing is literally broken by the missing article — the gap shows up instead as abbreviations that are never expanded anywhere in the zone.
